title: Can Opcode Sequences Reveal Malware Behavior? An Empirical Study of Classification, Semantic Compression, and Functional Interpretability
content: Malware continues to pose a significant threat within the cybersecurity landscape. While numerous detection algorithms have demonstrated high accuracy, the lack of interpretability in these models limits their practical applicability in high-stakes environments. This work explores the potential of opcode sequences, derived from disassembled binaries, not only for effective malware classification but also for revealing underlying malicious behaviors. Our study is driven by three core hypotheses: (1) opcode sequences are inherently separable forclassification, (2) dimensionality reduction can preserve semantic meaning, and (3) function- level opcode sequences are interpretable and can be mapped to human- understandablebehavior. To validate the first hypothesis, we implemented a simple artificial neural network(ANN) classifier, achieving 93% validation accuracy, 96% precision, and 90% recall. These results support the discriminative power of opcode sequences. For the second hypothesis, we developed a Wasserstein Autoencoder(WAE), which achieved near-lossless reconstruction with a reconstruction loss of 8.31 × 10−6and a Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) loss of 0.41603. This demonstrates effective semantic compression. To address the third hypothesis, we constructed a behaviorally annotated dataset by pairing opcode sequences with descriptions using large language DeepSeek-70B model via OLLAMA. The model successfully identified various malware traits, including unpacking routines, register manipulation for communication, anti-analysis techniques, system call usage, and obfuscation patterns. This study, provides promising evidence that opcode-level analysis can serve as a foundation for both accurate detection and transparent interpretation of malware behavior.
